text: President Xi Jinping told the opening of the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai on 17 July that the world needs a just and equitable system for governing AI, and announced a World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation with 29 founding member countries plus joint AI application centres to be built with ASEAN, the League of Arab States, the African Union, CELAC, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and BRICS.

Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn set out the bloc's approach to AI governance at the high-level meeting held alongside that Shanghai conference on 18 July, saying governments, international organisations, industry and universities will all be needed to handle what is coming.

The African Union Commission and Smart Africa agreed in Geneva on 20 July to coordinate delivery of the Continental AI Strategy, with an action plan, a financing plan and AI governance guidelines in preparation, alongside a proposed African Union AI fund and a pan-African AI centre.

Forum ICT ministers met in Port Moresby on 24 July with Papua New Guinea taking the chair, and put artificial intelligence, safer online spaces and how the region measures its own digital progress on the agenda under the Lagatoi Declaration.

The Caribbean Telecommunications Union closed its Caribbean Artificial Intelligence Forum in Trinidad and Tobago on 25 July and released the Caribbean AI Task Force report, which asks CARICOM states to harmonise AI policy and treat data sovereignty as a shared regional asset.

At the UN Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in July, delegates from Sami, Inuit and Ojibwe organisations argued that data centre projects should have to meet the standard of free, prior and informed consent, citing a Chilean environmental tribunal's suspension of a Google site in Santiago and a complaint brought by the Anace people against a data centre in north-east Brazil.

Five coalitions published a joint read-out of the opening session of the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance on 24 July, reporting that women and Indigenous Peoples were insufficiently represented across the talks and that chances for governments and other stakeholders to speak to each other directly stayed limited.

Two artificial intelligence bills, one in the Senate and one in the Chamber of Representatives, had cleared committee and remained in play as of 16 July, setting out rules for the development and supervision of AI systems with the science ministry to lead implementation.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on 15 July that large data centres will be required to underwrite their own new power supply, pay their share of connection costs and meet water efficiency standards under a mandatory national framework, to be put to national cabinet next month and to parliament early next year.

Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order on 15 July halting new state environmental permits for data centres while regulators take up to a year to write rules on energy use, water use and protections for surrounding communities.

Two county council committees voted on 22 July to advance an 18-month pause on new data centres and zoning that would block any facility above 25 megawatts, backed on the record by a coalition of more than 30 community, environmental and faith groups.
A UN News report on the Secretary-General's governance call was mostly about autonomous weapons, so it is not logged here.

The law implementing the EU AI Act in Germany, the KI-MIG, entered into force on 29 July and makes the Bundesnetzagentur the country's market surveillance authority, single contact point and complaints body for artificial intelligence, with direct oversight of systems used in employment, critical infrastructure and education.

The Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment announced on 30 July that the AI Office of Ireland has been established as an independent statutory body under the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act signed on 21 July, with Paul Byrne appointed as its first chief executive and the office due to be operational by 2 August.

The European Commission opened bidding on 30 July for up to seven AI gigafactories across the bloc, backed by about 10 billion euros of public money and an expected 30 billion euros in total once private investment is counted, with consortia given until 12 November to apply and awards due in early 2027.

The Ministry of Science and ICT launched an AI data centre alliance on 29 July, co-chaired by the minister and the chief executive of SK Telecom, bringing twelve companies together behind a national target of 18.4 gigawatts of data centre capacity by 2035.

The National AI Office closed its public consultation on a proposed AI Governance Bill on 31 July, after three weeks open from 10 July, on a law that would apply to AI systems placed on the market, developed or used in Malaysia.

Digital and AI ministers from the 21 APEC economies met in Chengdu on 23 July and issued a joint statement backing human-centred and locally tailored AI, voluntary experience sharing and technical assistance, while recording that members take different approaches to their own AI policies.

President José Raúl Mulino launched the National Advanced Technologies Agenda on 30 July, whose AI strategy rests on six pillars including data governance and AI ethics and regulation, and which sits alongside a bill on adaptive governance of artificial intelligence now before the National Assembly.

The Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy opened public participation on 27 July on a draft Artificial Intelligence and Other Emerging Technologies Policy, taking written submissions from institutions, industry, academia, civil society and the public until 4 August.

The government approved a 170 million US dollar project reported on 24 July for a sovereign data centre, a government digital platform and a smart border system, to be delivered with Cisco and Cybastion.

The county quorum court voted 10 to 3 on 28 July against a twelve month pause on data centre construction, and separately rejected by 8 to 6 an amendment that would have required the AVAIO Digital project near Wrightsville to meet any future county rules before its later phases.

County leaders held a standing room only public forum on data centres on 28 July, at which the judge executive said every person present raised a hand against them and reported a survey of 1,500 residents in which 80 per cent said no, ahead of a fiscal court vote on a moratorium set for 11 August.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, entered into force on 27 July and amends the AI Act to push stand-alone high-risk obligations from 2 August 2026 back to 2 December 2027 and embedded high-risk systems from 2 August 2027 back to 2 August 2028, while adding two prohibited practices from 2 December 2026 covering AI that generates non-consensual intimate images and child sexual abuse material.

Public comment closed on 31 July on a proposed Federal Trade Commission policy statement on accuracy in AI systems, which argues that state laws appearing to coerce companies into altering the output of their models, naming Colorado's Artificial Intelligence Act, may be impliedly preempted by federal law.
The full county council voted unanimously on 28 July to adopt the 18-month pause on new data centre permits, moving it past the committee stage logged here on 22 July.

The state congress repealed the artificial intelligence provisions of the state penal code on 30 July, striking the chapter on improper use of AI to cause social alarm, and Governor Ricardo Gallardo Cardona said a broader AI law would be drafted this year with academics, health specialists and psychologists.

The European Commission's AI Office and national authorities began enforcing the AI Act on 2 August, and from the same day interactive AI systems must tell people they are dealing with a machine, deepfakes must be labelled, and AI-generated or edited content must carry machine-readable marks so it can be detected.

About a dozen AI companies were shown a finalised voluntary framework at the White House on 4 August under which developers would give the federal government access to closed frontier models 30 days before release, and the administration said it does not plan to publish the framework.

The World Bank released World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence on 4 August, reporting that 4.5 per cent of jobs in developing economies are exposed to automation by generative AI against 14.2 per cent in high income countries, and that nearly a third of rural schools in Sub-Saharan Africa still lack reliable electricity.

The Senate's science and technology committee held a public hearing on 4 August on a bill to regulate data centres, at which the Anace cacique Roberto Anace described them as a new colonisation, the Consumer Defence Institute warned that round the clock demand raises electricity costs for everyone, and a researcher from INESC said the environmental burden stays in the country while the services are exported.

Reuters reported on 6 August that the Andhra Pradesh High Court has told the state government to answer a challenge to the 15 billion US dollar Google and Adani data centre hub at Visakhapatnam, where the Kambalakonda wildlife sanctuary sits 860 metres from the site and the city draws 410 million litres of water a day against a requirement of 480 million.

Prism reported on 5 August that the Seminole Nation has approved a moratorium on AI data centre development, the Cherokee Nation has set up a task force following an executive order signed by Principal Chief Chuck Hoskin Jr in February, and the Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation is holding tribal councils on a proposed 10,000 acre site in Utah.

President Claudia Sheinbaum told her morning press conference on 10 August that she was struck to learn young people use artificial intelligence as a psychologist, and said regional forums with parents, teachers and specialists, starting 19 August in Nuevo Leon, will produce a bill to Congress on children's use of digital platforms and AI.
The Senate Commerce Committee voted on 5 August to advance the CHATBOT Act, a bill by Ted Cruz and Brian Schatz that would give parents controls over how their children interact with AI companions.

Town commissioners voted unanimously on 3 August for a twelve month freeze on data centres after a public hearing at which residents objected on environmental grounds and over rising energy bills, and the mayor said the pause is for gathering information rather than a decision against any future facility.

Public participation on the draft Artificial Intelligence and Other Emerging Technologies Policy closed on 4 August, the deadline set when the ministry opened it on 27 July, and the draft proposes a National AI and Other Emerging Technologies Council with a governing board, a technical advisory forum and five directorates.

TechAfrica News reported on 6 August that Eduardo Mondlane University in Maputo has opened a solar powered data centre for research, cybersecurity and AI work, and that the Minister of Communications and Digital Transformation, Americo Muchanga, asked universities to take over management of the national research and education network.

Colorado's House Bill 26-1263, which requires operators of conversational artificial intelligence services to disclose that the service is not a person, run a self-harm response protocol and estimate user age, entered into force on 12 August, with its content moderation duties for minors following on 1 January 2027.

Public comment on the draft Anti Cyber Violence Law closed on 28 August, a month after the Cyberspace Administration of China put the text out on 29 July, the draft requiring platforms to trace, remove, block and report to the authorities cyberbullying content that is generated or spread using artificial intelligence, to run automated detection, and to give users a one click protection feature, with fines up to 10 million yuan, and with a site, an application or a business licence able to be shut down or withdrawn for serious or repeat breaches.

Morocco and India agreed in Rabat on 24 August to set up a joint commission on languages and digital technologies, with large language models named as its subject, at the seventh session of the Morocco India Joint Commission attended by Morocco's minister delegate for digital transition and administration reform, Amal El Fallah Seghrouchni, and India's minister of state for commerce and industry and for electronics and information technology, Jitin Prasada, the first stated aim being to carry Moroccan Darija and Amazigh into Idarati, the platform Moroccans use to reach government services online, with Seghrouchni pointing to an Indian application that already works in 28 languages.

The National Data Protection Authority argued in public on 26 August for the quick passage of an artificial intelligence law, its superintendent for technological innovation Lucas Costa dos Anjos telling a panel at Febraban Tech in Sao Paulo that a bill is needed because it would bring more legal certainty to the whole ecosystem, and that while the general data protection law already carries rules that reach artificial intelligence, a new law would add protection for people whose rights could be breached, with the country still working without a dedicated artificial intelligence statute while the authority runs a regulatory sandbox in the gap.

The Pataskala city council voted seven to nil on 25 August to reject the site plan for a 200 megawatt, three building campus proposed by Aligned Data Centers in the city's industrial park, council members saying they could not vote on plans that did not yet say how the site would be powered, because that question falls to the Ohio Power Siting Board only after the city approves, and that they would not make decisions based on guesses, with the developer having put the project at more than 100 permanent jobs and more than 5 billion United States dollars, and with voters in Pataskala and Granville due to decide a proposed ban on large data centres at the ballot on 3 November.

The California legislature sent four artificial intelligence bills to the governor between 24 and 26 August, ahead of its 31 August adjournment: AB 2656, which would require state and local public employers to give written notice to employee organisations at least 45 days before bringing in generative artificial intelligence that affects represented jobs, passed on concurrence 74 votes to 2; SB 503, which would require developers and deployers of medical clinical decision support tools to find and reduce biased effects, passed 39 to nil; AB 2392, which would have the state's universities convene a joint working group on procurement standards for generative artificial intelligence by 1 January 2028, passed the Senate 38 to nil; and AB 2025, which would require disclosure when artificial intelligence has altered promotional material for real property, passed the Senate 39 to 1 and the Assembly 78 to nil.

Bloomberg reported on 26 August that political opposition is slowing data centre growth and pushing developers and the firms funding them to take community objections into account, citing the investment firm Kimmeridge Energy Management for an estimate that as many as half the data centres proposed in the United States are at risk of delay or cancellation, and McKinsey for the observation that the backlash is real enough that some operators are abandoning sites they have already spent money on.

body: Dropped as older than the window
text: Six organisations, among them Accion Civica, the Latin American Observatory of Environmental Conflicts and human rights clinics at Virginia and Anglia Ruskin universities, asked the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights on 21 August to make Chile explain Supreme Decree 17/2025, published on 21 January 2026, which lifted the fuel storage threshold that triggers environmental assessment from 80 tonnes to 1,000 tonnes and narrowed the electrical infrastructure trigger, and which lets the 200 million United States dollar Cerrillos data centre proceed without assessment after an environmental court had partly revoked its permits over water. That is two days outside the seven day window, so it is recorded rather than logged as current, and it is the clearest thing found this week for both open questions.

The Caribbean, the Middle East and North Africa, and Europe beyond items already on this page produced nothing inside the window, searched by name and in Spanish, Portuguese and Arabic as well as English. Brazil's PL 2338 is still with the Chamber of Deputies special committee, Kenya's draft artificial intelligence and emerging technologies policy closed for public comment on 4 August, Malaysia's artificial intelligence governance bill consultation closed on 31 July, and the African Union's continental strategy produced nothing new in the window. Correcting the 29 August note: PACNEWS has published editions on 25, 26, 27 and 28 August, so the claim that none had appeared since 21 August was wrong; none of those editions carried an artificial intelligence or data centre item.

body: Nothing excluded under the defence rule
text: No item found in this window was primarily military or defence.

The Government Leadership and Artificial Intelligence Summit opens in Abuja today, 31 August, as the first of four days of GITEX Nigeria running on to Lagos until 3 September, with more than 150 federal and state agencies due to work through digital identity, cybersecurity, digital governance, connectivity and digital public services, the event held under the theme Beyond Connectivity, The Bridge to Sovereign Innovation and supported by the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy with the National Information Technology Development Agency, and the minister, Bosun Tijani, putting the case that Nigeria and the wider continent should become producers of technology and of the solutions built on it.

Five organisations, the Housing Assembly, Foxglove, Open Secrets, Research + Action and the Planetary AI Collective, with legal analysis from Open Secrets and the Legal Resources Centre, put a joint submission to the South African Human Rights Commission on 24 August asking it to hold a national public inquiry that would end in a rule requiring every facility to disclose its water and electricity use, to commission an independent assessment of the sector's human rights, ecological and economic effects, to pause new hyperscale approvals until that inquiry reports, and to set up an independent monitoring panel with power to enforce, the submission putting the approved Equinix facilities in Cape Town at more than 4.4 billion litres of water a year, about what 18,000 South African households use, with four fifths of it lost to evaporation, and noting that Eskom's roughly 6 gigawatt surplus, generated overwhelmingly by coal, is being marketed to data centre operators without any requirement that they build matching clean generation, after Cape Town's Municipal Planning Tribunal approved the rezoning on 14 July with one member dissenting for want of information.

An investigation published on 27 August found the part built DataOne artificial intelligence data centre, about 40 miles from Philadelphia, running at least 45 of its 62 tractor trailer sized generators at once in mid August, established by thermal drone footage, with a New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection spokesperson saying the department has issued no permits for power generators at the site and has none under review, and Bruce Buckheit, a former head of air enforcement at the United States Environmental Protection Agency, saying the activity violates federal law and the company should stop the generators and pay a fine, while DataOne declined to answer questions on the generators and said it remains committed to meeting all applicable environmental and permitting requirements, and Microsoft, which draws computing from the site under a 17 billion United States dollar agreement with the Dutch infrastructure company Nebius, did not respond.

Governor Mikie Sherrill signed Senate Bill 3379 into law on 27 August at the South Brunswick Public Library, requiring every data centre owner and operator in the state to file a report with the Board of Public Utilities every six months for three years covering total energy use, the energy going to cooling and to computing equipment, peak daily water use, where the water comes from and what backup power is held on site, the bill having passed the Assembly 76 votes to 3 and the Senate 39 to nil at the end of June, and the signing completing the four part plan the governor set out in May; residents and critics have called the self reporting requirement too weak and are asking for a statewide ban, with dozens of New Jersey municipalities having already barred data centres outright.

body: Dropped as older than it looked
text: A data centre digest listed the Tallahassee city commission's 3 to 2 refusal of a one year pause on large data centres as a 27 August action, and the vote was actually on 11 June 2026. A State Council directive deepening China's Artificial Intelligence Plus initiative surfaced in searches as an August item; it was published on 26 August 2025, a year outside the window. A Pakistani industry association's objection to the draft National Data Governance Policy carried two different dates in two outlets, 12 August and 27 August, so it is left out rather than logged on a date that could not be settled.

The 30 August entry said the 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting opened in Koror on 30 August. Leaders gathered in Palau across the weekend and the meeting formally opens on 31 August, running to 4 September. The Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles are still before leaders, and today's Forum coverage carried no artificial intelligence or data centre item.

Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, the Middle East and North Africa, Europe, and the Pacific beyond the Forum produced nothing inside the window, searched by name and in Spanish, Portuguese and Arabic as well as English. What is standing rather than moving: Thailand's public hearing on its redrafted artificial intelligence act closed on 14 August, Pakistan's draft data governance policy has been open since 26 June, Johor's restrictions on water hungry data centres date to late 2025, Brazil's PL 2338 still sits with the Chamber of Deputies special committee, the CARICOM roadmap was endorsed on 7 July, and Bangladesh's draft policy consultation closed on 8 February.
Nothing was left out under the defence rule today: no item found in this window was primarily military or defence.

Version 2.0 of the Guideline for Japanese Governments' Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI for the sake of Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration enters into force today, 1 September, having been put out for public comment from 18 March to 8 April 2026 and approved by the Council for the Promotion of a Digital Society on 12 June, and it requires every ministry to appoint a Chief Artificial Intelligence Officer, to run a risk assessment on each generative artificial intelligence system, to buy against set check sheets, and to report any project likely to be classed high risk to the Advanced AI Utilization Advisory Board.

Submissions to the Senate Environment and Communications References Committee inquiry into artificial intelligence and data centres close today, 1 September, the inquiry having begun in May under the chair of Senator Sarah Hanson-Young to look at whether existing regulation keeps pace with the growth of data centres and at their effects on communities, industries and the environment, with a report due on 16 November 2026 and submissions already lodged by the Local Government Association of South Australia, the Climate Council, Climateworks Centre and the ARC Centre of Excellence for Automated Decision-Making and Society.

An analysis published on 28 August argued that Aboriginal people are being left out of decisions on where artificial intelligence data centres go, citing the 120 megawatt project at Mandoon Bilya on the Helena River in Perth's eastern suburbs that was withdrawn in May 2026 before Western Australia's Development Assessment Panel could consider it, after a campaign led by the Bibbul Ngarma Aboriginal Association over Aboriginal heritage sites and the river, with more than 200 people planting over 3,000 native plants there in July, and quoting Kaley Nicholson, chief executive of the Federation of Victorian Traditional Owner Corporations, calling the current approach an investment failure, while pointing to the Karajarri People as co-owners of Western Australia's largest data centre through an Indigenous Land Use Agreement and to Traditional Owner engagement on a hyperscale project in the Northern Territory.

The Ministry of Science and ICT announced on 28 August that it had chosen three consortiums, led by SK Telecom, KT and Kakao, from six applicants to run the AI for All project, which is to give every one of the country's roughly 52 million people free access to artificial intelligence tools, with the operators required to use models built by other companies alongside their own, receiving a combined 512 Nvidia B200 graphics processing units from the government this year and part of their running costs from 2027, agreements due to be signed in September and a full launch planned for December.

The Elkhart city council voted nine to nil on Thursday 27 August at a special meeting to stop accepting applications for data centres and battery storage facilities until the council lifts the pause or 31 December 2027, whichever comes first, councillors saying they need the time to study the effects and to write rules on noise, water and electricity, and Mayor Rod Roberson saying it is not a rejection of data centres but a pause to look at what they mean for the community, with the pause applying to the city and not the county.

The Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy, Andrew Charlton, launched the Buy Australian AI Partnership on 27 August, an eight week accelerator run by Stone and Chalk with the National AI Centre that puts Australian artificial intelligence companies in front of buyers in banking, insurance and superannuation, with the Commonwealth Bank, Westpac, ANZ, NAB and Cuscal helping participants work through enterprise procurement, assurance, regulatory requirements and deployment, the first intake aimed at financial services.

The Ministry of Law and the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore opened a public consultation on 26 August on how artificial intelligence should be handled in the country's intellectual property regime, running to 22 October and open to anyone, covering the use of copyright material to train models, copyright risk when models are deployed, what counts as human creativity in a work made with artificial intelligence, who can be named an inventor when a person and a machine work together, and what machine generated technical disclosures do to the field of prior art.

Left out under the defence rule: a United Kingdom and Ukraine information sharing partnership reported on 25 August that would give the United Kingdom access to Ukrainian battlefield data through the Avengers AI Labs to train models, and a United States federal court ruling of 26 August on the Department of Defense blacklisting of Anthropic. A third was a closer call and is recorded rather than logged: Huawei filed a bid on 26 August to build artificial intelligence data centres in Egypt, and the sectors named for it include defence, security and public surveillance alongside civil government, so it sits on the line the rule draws.

Dropped as older than the seven day window: the New Mexico Supreme Court paused the air quality permit hearing for the Oracle and OpenAI Project Jupiter campus in Dona Ana County and stopped the State Engineer allowing a well to supply the site's construction water, on a petition by New Energy Economy, with the hearing officer Max Shepherd recusing himself the same weekend after the Center for Biological Diversity and the New Mexico Environmental Law Center moved to disqualify him; all of that fell on 23 and 24 August. Councillors in Centre Wellington, Ontario voted unanimously on 24 August for a one year data centre pause, returning for formal approval on 28 September. Kokomo, Indiana passed its data centre standards ordinance on first reading six votes to two on 24 August. A Daily Maverick investigation into South African data centre approvals ran on 24 August.

Leaders of the ten member states signed the Bishkek Declaration on 1 September at the close of the 26th summit in Kyrgyzstan, marking the organisation's 25th year, and alongside it signed a Memorandum among the Governments of SCO Member States on Cooperation in the Field of Artificial Intelligence and a Concept for the Establishment of Regional Data Processing Centres, Computing Capacities and the Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry within the SCO, with the declaration calling for the responsible use of artificial intelligence and the summit producing about 28 documents in all; the members signing are Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.

At the Lagos leg of GITEX Nigeria on 1 September the director general of the National Information Technology Development Agency, Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, said artificial intelligence sovereignty has to cover the whole chain from connectivity and computing capacity through data centres, cloud infrastructure and data governance to the models themselves, warning against foreign controlled systems settling into finance and health, while the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, George Akume, named three instruments the country is leaning on: Project Bridge, a fibre build of about 90,000 kilometres, the Three Million Technical Talent programme with 1.87 million registrations, and a National Digital Cloud Policy seeking 750 million United States dollars of private cloud investment over 24 months. This page logged the Abuja opening of the same event on 31 August; what is new is the sovereignty framing and the cloud policy figure.

The Coalizao Direitos na Rede, which speaks for more than 50 organisations, together with the Laboratorio de Politicas Publicas e Internet, the Instituto de Defesa do Consumidor and the Rede pela Soberania Digital, published a public note on 31 August objecting to about 7.2 billion reais of tax exemptions for data centres under Bill 278 of 2026, the Redata regime, being granted before the country has rules to go with them, arguing that sovereignty means national technological and scientific capability, data security and governance, energy autonomy and protection of natural resources, and asking for more negotiation, discussions held in the open, and obligations on the companies that benefit rather than servers placed on Brazilian soil; the bill stood first on the Senate's order paper for the sitting of 1 September, and if the Senate passes it the text goes to the president for signature.

The second phase of the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum's call for input on consumer interest and artificial intelligence closes today, 2 September, this phase asking anyone who wishes to answer about the tools, governance frameworks and regulatory approaches available to policymakers, regulators and firms for reducing harms from generative and agentic artificial intelligence while still protecting consumers, the first phase having closed on 3 July after asking people which risks they feel exposed to and what they are willing to tolerate in exchange for the benefits.

County commissioners voted two in favour, none against and one abstaining on 31 August to approve the agreement for Google's first Kansas data centre, a 1.7 million square foot site near Sharon known as Project Helium, with the agreement requiring the facility to be closed loop and air cooled rather than water cooled and to buy any other water it needs from a regulated municipal utility, the company putting the site at 500 jobs once running and initial operations from 2030, and county estimates putting property tax at close to 10 million United States dollars a year, against a state exemption available to large data centres for up to 20 years.

The city council voted unanimously on 31 August for a resolution opposing data centre development inside the city limits and calling for further study of the effects on utilities, infrastructure, public safety and the city's economic goals, with no application before it and council members pointing to the statewide pause on approvals the governor ordered on 3 August, pending an audit by the Public Utility Commission of Texas and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, as the reason to act ahead of one.

Dropped as older than the window: China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said on 26 August that the country has formulated close to 200 key standards for artificial intelligence covering foundational technologies, application requirements and safety ethics, and that 6G work is being brought forward into the 2026 to 2030 plan period; China is a big power on this page's shorter window, so at seven days it is recorded rather than logged. Wixom, Michigan ended its six month data centre pause by vote on 26 August, adopting setbacks of 1,500 feet from homes, parks and schools and a ban on well water, with the rules to start no later than 6 September and a developer suing over the original pause.

Left out under the defence rule: the Bishkek summit's security documents, which take up most of the 28 signed, including counter-terrorism and counter-narcotics instruments. Only the artificial intelligence memorandum, the regional data centre concept and the declaration's line on responsible use are logged.

United States commerce secretary Howard Lutnick said at the close of the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina on 2 September that all of the group's member nations had endorsed the Carolina Principles, a framework drafted by the United States under which governments agree to reserve new regulation for novel considerations rather than write rules specific to artificial intelligence, to direct funding towards foundational research and to widen commercial openings for emerging technologies, with White House science and technology policy director Michael Kratsios telling the meeting that policymakers do not need to approach each innovation in isolation and should not treat every emerging technology as a first of its kind policy problem, and Lutnick saying that getting every country to agree had taken an enormous amount of work.

body: Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States
text: Several hundred students, retired staff and residents marched outside the same Chapel Hill meeting on 2 September, organised by the University of North Carolina chapters of the Sunrise Movement, Students for Justice in Palestine and the NAACP together with the Campus Y and the Party for Socialism and Liberation, calling for more government regulation of artificial intelligence and objecting to the environmental effect of the infrastructure, to surveillance cameras on campus and to the part technology executives are playing in setting policy, with speakers questioning the university's decision to host the summit.

The European Commission said on 1 September it had sent requests for information to more than 30 companies working in artificial intelligence, asking providers how they defend models against attack, whether independent experts have assessed them, how systems are watched after release and what the training data contains, a step that can precede a formal investigation under the AI Act, with spokesman Thomas Regnier saying the questionnaires concerned mostly safety and copyright and vice president for technology sovereignty Henna Virkkunen saying the Commission is ready to take all necessary steps to ensure companies comply with their obligations.

The Green Party of England and Wales, led by Zack Polanski, called on 1 September for a moratorium on most new data centres across the United Kingdom with an exemption for smaller local scale sites, and asked for mandatory reporting of water and electricity use, tougher environmental standards and more community involvement in planning decisions, citing about 1,125 megalitres of water a year across roughly 200 English sites, under one per cent of non household use, and a 170 per cent rise in data centre water use in the South East between 2021 and 2025; the government rejected the moratorium, saying a halt would damage jobs and national security, and disputed the claim that data centres would be given priority over households during a shortage.

The Senate approved Bill 278 of 2026 on 1 September by symbolic vote, creating Redata, a special tax regime that suspends federal taxes including import duty, IPI, PIS/Pasep and Cofins on information technology equipment for companies building or expanding data centres in Brazil, with revenue forgone estimated at 7.25 billion reais to 2028, and conditions requiring all electricity to come from renewable or low emission sources, 2 per cent of the value of equipment bought to be invested in research and development inside Brazil and at least 10 per cent of processing and storage capacity reserved for the domestic market, with a 20 per cent reduction in the investment requirement for sites in the North, Northeast and Central West; the bill now goes to the president for signature. This page logged the objection from the Coalizao Direitos na Rede and three other groups on 2 September; what has changed is that the bill has passed and the conditions attached to it are settled text.

Egypt's Central Auditing Organisation, whose head Mohamed Al Faisal Youssef also chairs the International Organisation of Supreme Audit Institutions, issued 15 recommendations on 1 September on how national audit bodies should govern their own use of artificial intelligence, among them choosing resource efficient models rather than assuming larger ones are better, putting data governance, cybersecurity, transparency and ethics in place before deployment, introducing the technology gradually in proportion to each body's capacity, keeping it as a support to the auditor rather than a replacement, tying each application to stated objectives with measurable indicators, and building skills at three levels: specialists, competent users and general awareness.

Two national rules touching artificial intelligence took effect on 1 September: a national standard on coordination between human and machine customer service, which makes companies legally responsible for what their automated customer service says, so that a reply being machine generated is not a defence, and requires a working transfer to a person; and management measures for micro short dramas, which require a clearly visible label on every episode made with artificial intelligence.

The Collaboratory for Indigenous Data Governance held a six speaker panel on 2 September introducing its new Guidelines for the Governance of Indigenous Peoples' Data in Scholarly Publishing, part of a webinar series whose 26 August session heard Margaret Yun-Pu Tu on Indigenous data sovereignty in Taiwan.

Dropped as older than the window: the Alberta Court of King's Bench ruling of 13 August that let Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation proceed to judicial review of the water licence for the Wonder Valley project, which is already carried on the ahead list for December; and an analysis published on 28 August on Traditional Owner exclusion from Australian data centre planning, which reports the cancellation in May of a 120 megawatt site on the Mandoon Bilya in Western Australia and objections in Victoria, both older than the window for an English language source. Judged too routine to log: Michigan City, Indiana approved four data centre resolutions on 2 September amid local opposition, ordinary local tax and zoning business rather than a change in how decisions get made.
